text: how realistic do you think it is to add higher order differentiation to treams-rs?

items.html:
Very realistic for second derivatives and Hessian–vector products. Arbitrary-order differentiation across the whole API would be a substantially larger project. Having inspected the current code, I think a useful second-order implementation could preserve the existing architecture.

The main obstacle is the derivative boundary. Rust computes an analytic pullback, but that pullback is opaque to the framework: JAX calls it through pure_callback, and PyTorch explicitly rejects higher-order gradients. Supporting another derivative requires differentiating the pullback itself, including its dependence on both the original inputs and the incoming cotangent. This is an established extension pattern; PyTorch documents double backward through external numerical code.

The numerical foundations are encouraging:

  • Linear solves are a good fit. For (Ax=b), the directional derivative satisfies (A\dot{x}=\dot{b}-\dot{A}x). Additional derivatives can use additional solves with the same factorization. The existing adjoint already reuses the forward LU.
  • Some local second derivatives already exist. Radial Bessel kernels return value, first and second derivatives. That helps, although formulas already containing Bessel derivatives can require third derivatives for second-order sensitivity.
  • The general jets need extending. Jet<N> stores first derivatives in N directions; increasing N does not increase derivative order. Its concrete complex scalar also means nesting jets is not currently a drop-in solution.

My assessment of scope is:

Target Assessment
Second derivatives of selected special functions and solves Straightforward, bounded work
Hessian–vector products through sphere/cluster scattering objectives Very achievable; meaningful kernel and adapter work
Broad coverage including periodic sums, fields and eigenmodes Substantial implementation and numerical validation
Arbitrary nested derivatives everywhere A larger derivative-system design commitment

I would start with Hessian–vector products through one complete scattering objective, with radii and material parameters, then add particle positions and interactions. Keep the derivative calculations in Rust, expose the required directional derivatives and differentiated pullbacks, and prove composition through one adapter first. Avoid forming dense Hessians.

The difficult part will be trustworthy coverage: complex-gradient conventions, derivative convergence of lattice sums, and conditioning near resonances. Diffraction thresholds and individual eigenmodes at degeneracies also impose mathematical limits that additional autodiff machinery cannot remove.

My rough engineering estimate is weeks for a useful scoped second-order implementation, months for broad validated coverage. I’d use the first complete workflow to refine that estimate.

I inspected the source and ran three existing tests confirming the current higher-order rejection behavior; all passed. No code changed, and higher-order correctness or performance has not yet been demonstrated.
